q: A 58-year-old woman presents with a 4-month history of symmetrical pain and early-morning stiffness lasting 2 hours affecting the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints of both hands and both wrists. On examination there is soft-tissue swelling and tenderness of six small joints. She has no psoriasis or nail changes. Investigations: ESR 48 mm/h, CRP 32 mg/L, rheumatoid factor negative, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibody strongly positive at 240 U/mL (normal <7). Radiographs of the hands show periarticular osteopenia but no erosions. Which single feature carries the greatest weight for a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis and predicts the most erosive disease course?
options: Symmetrical small-joint distribution
Early-morning stiffness exceeding 1 hour
Elevated ESR and CRP
Strongly positive anti-CCP antibody
Periarticular osteopenia on radiographs
explain: 🎯 Anti-CCP antibody is the single most specific serological marker for rheumatoid arthritis (~95% specificity) and is the strongest predictor of erosive, progressive disease. Mechanism: peptidylarginine deiminase citrullinates arginine residues in synovial proteins (fibrin, vimentin, filaggrin); in genetically susceptible individuals (HLA-DRB1 shared epitope), citrullinated peptides break tolerance, generating anti-CCP antibodies years before symptom onset. These antibodies drive osteoclast activation and immune-complex inflammation. In the 2010 ACR/EULAR classification criteria, a high-titre ACPA (>3× upper limit) scores the maximum 3 points in the serology domain — more than RF. This patient is seronegative for RF but strongly ACPA-positive, confirming disease and flagging a poor prognosis warranting early DMARD therapy. Symmetry, stiffness >1 h, and raised acute-phase reactants support the diagnosis but are non-specific. Periarticular osteopenia is an early radiographic change but lacks prognostic weight compared with ACPA. Per NICE NG100, early referral and methotrexate within 3 months of persistent synovitis is indicated. 🩺

q: A 26-year-old woman presents with a malar rash, oral ulcers, and pain in the small joints of the hands. Blood tests show haemoglobin 98 g/L, white cells 2.8 ×10⁹/L, lymphocytes 0.7 ×10⁹/L, and platelets 95 ×10⁹/L. Urinalysis shows protein 2+ and red-cell casts. ANA is positive at a titre of 1:1280 with a homogeneous pattern. Complement C3 and C4 are both reduced. Which single autoantibody is most specific for systemic lupus erythematosus and correlates best with lupus nephritis activity?
options: Anti-Ro (SSA) antibody
Anti-double-stranded DNA antibody
Anti-histone antibody
Anti-U1-RNP antibody
Anti-Sm antibody
explain: 🎯 Anti-dsDNA is highly specific for SLE (~95%) and, crucially, its titre fluctuates with disease activity, particularly renal involvement. Mechanism: anti-dsDNA immune complexes deposit in the glomerular basement membrane, activating the classical complement pathway — this is why C3 and C4 fall during active nephritis. Rising anti-dsDNA with falling complement is the classic serological signature of a lupus nephritis flare and guides immunosuppression. Anti-Sm is even more specific (~99%) but is present in only ~20–30% of patients and does not track disease activity, so it is a diagnostic marker rather than a monitoring tool. This patient meets EULAR/ACR 2019 criteria (positive ANA as entry, plus haematological, mucocutaneous, renal and immunological domains). Anti-Ro is associated with Sjögren's, subacute cutaneous lupus and neonatal lupus/congenital heart block. Anti-histone antibodies suggest drug-induced lupus. Anti-U1-RNP at high titre defines mixed connective tissue disease. Renal biopsy remains essential to classify ISN/RPS class and direct therapy. 🩺

q: A 72-year-old woman presents with a 3-week history of new-onset left-sided temporal headache, scalp tenderness on brushing her hair, and jaw pain when chewing. She reports transient blurring of vision in the left eye yesterday. Examination shows a tender, thickened, non-pulsatile left temporal artery. ESR is 88 mm/h and CRP 96 mg/L. Her visual acuity is currently normal. Which is the single most appropriate immediate management step?
options: Start high-dose oral prednisolone 60 mg daily immediately
Arrange temporal artery biopsy before any treatment
Start oral prednisolone 15 mg daily and review in one week
Arrange urgent temporal artery ultrasound before treatment
Commence intravenous tocilizumab as first-line therapy
explain: 🎯 This is giant cell arteritis (GCA) with visual symptoms (amaurosis fugax) — an ophthalmic emergency. The overriding priority is to prevent irreversible anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy in the fellow eye, so high-dose glucocorticoids must be started immediately without waiting for any investigation. Per BSR guidelines, patients with visual symptoms should receive high-dose steroids (often IV methylprednisolone 500 mg–1 g for evolving/established visual loss, or oral prednisolone 40–60 mg if no established loss) urgently. Mechanism: GCA is a granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis of the aorta and its branches; Th1/Th17-driven inflammation with giant cells causes intimal hyperplasia and occlusion of the ophthalmic/posterior ciliary arteries. Crucially, steroids do not abolish biopsy positivity for up to 2 weeks, so treatment must never be delayed for biopsy or ultrasound — these confirm the diagnosis but should follow, not precede, treatment. Temporal artery biopsy (or halo sign on ultrasound) is arranged promptly but after steroids. Tocilizumab (IL-6 receptor antagonist) is a steroid-sparing agent for relapsing/refractory disease, not initial monotherapy. 🩺

q: A 45-year-old woman with a 10-year history of Raynaud's phenomenon presents with tightening of the skin over her fingers and face, telangiectasia, and difficulty swallowing solids. She has no proximal skin involvement above the elbows or knees. Nailfold capillaroscopy shows dilated capillary loops. Anti-centromere antibody is positive. She is well with normal renal function and blood pressure. Which single complication is she at greatest long-term risk of developing?
options: Scleroderma renal crisis
Rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease
Pulmonary arterial hypertension
Myocardial fibrosis with heart block
Gastric antral vascular ectasia bleeding
explain: 🎯 This is limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (formerly CREST), defined by skin involvement distal to elbows/knees plus the face, a long Raynaud's prodrome, and anti-centromere antibodies. The characteristic late complication of the limited subtype is isolated pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), which typically develops after many years and is the leading cause of death in this group. Mechanism: a vasculopathy with intimal proliferation and obliteration of pulmonary arterioles raises pulmonary vascular resistance, independent of parenchymal lung fibrosis. Annual screening with echocardiography and pulmonary function tests (isolated fall in DLCO) is recommended so PAH is detected early and treated with endothelin-receptor antagonists, PDE-5 inhibitors or prostanoids. By contrast, diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (anti-Scl-70/topoisomerase and anti-RNA-polymerase III) carries the high risk of severe interstitial lung disease and scleroderma renal crisis. Renal crisis is strongly linked to anti-RNA-pol III and early diffuse disease — this anti-centromere-positive limited patient is at low renal risk. Anti-centromere positivity is in fact protective against renal crisis. 🩺

q: A 34-year-old woman is referred following her third first-trimester miscarriage. She also reports a previous unprovoked left calf deep vein thrombosis at age 30. Examination reveals a livedo reticularis rash. Blood tests: platelets 92 ×10⁹/L, activated partial thromboplastin time prolonged and not correcting on mixing studies. Lupus anticoagulant is positive, and anti-cardiolipin IgG is strongly positive; both are confirmed positive again 14 weeks later. She is not currently pregnant and has had no thrombosis for 3 years but remains on no treatment. Which is the single most appropriate long-term management for thromboprophylaxis?
options: Low-dose aspirin 75 mg daily alone
Lifelong warfarin with a target INR of 2.0–3.0
A direct oral anticoagulant such as rivaroxaban
Low-molecular-weight heparin only during future pregnancies
Hydroxychloroquine monotherapy
explain: 🎯 This woman has antiphospholipid syndrome (APS): a prior venous thrombosis plus recurrent pregnancy loss, with persistently positive lupus anticoagulant and anti-cardiolipin (confirmed >12 weeks apart, satisfying the Sydney criteria). Because she has had a definite thrombotic event, she needs lifelong anticoagulation with warfarin targeting an INR of 2.0–3.0. Mechanism: antiphospholipid antibodies (chiefly anti-β2-glycoprotein I) bind phospholipid–protein complexes on endothelium, platelets and trophoblast, activating complement and tissue factor, producing a prothrombotic state and placental insufficiency. The prolonged APTT that fails to correct on mixing reflects the in-vitro lupus anticoagulant effect, paradoxically associated with thrombosis, not bleeding. Crucially, the TRAPS trial and EULAR guidance show DOACs are inferior to warfarin in APS — especially triple-positive patients, where rivaroxaban increased arterial thrombotic events — so DOACs should be avoided. Aspirin alone is inadequate secondary prevention after venous thrombosis. LMWH plus aspirin is used during pregnancy (warfarin is teratogenic), but she is not pregnant. Hydroxychloroquine is adjunctive, not a substitute for anticoagulation. 🩺

q: A 38-year-old man presents with a 4-month history of recurrent epistaxis, nasal crusting, and a saddle-nose deformity. He has developed a cough with haemoptysis and progressive breathlessness. Blood tests show creatinine 210 μmol/L, and urinalysis reveals haematuria with red-cell casts. Chest radiograph shows bilateral nodular cavitating lesions. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody testing is positive with a cytoplasmic pattern, and antibodies against proteinase 3 (PR3) are strongly positive. Which single feature of this condition best distinguishes it from eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis?
options: Renal involvement with a pauci-immune glomerulonephritis
Positivity for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies
Response to glucocorticoid and cyclophosphamide therapy
Absence of asthma and peripheral blood eosinophilia
Involvement of the upper respiratory tract
explain: 🎯 This is granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) — the triad of upper airway (saddle nose, nasal crusting), lung (cavitating nodules, haemoptysis) and kidney (pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis), with cANCA/anti-PR3 positivity. The feature that most reliably separates GPA from eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA, Churg–Strauss) is the absence of asthma and eosinophilia. Mechanism/pattern: EGPA is defined by late-onset asthma, marked peripheral eosinophilia (>1.5 ×10⁹/L or >10%), and eosinophilic tissue infiltration; it is typically pANCA/anti-MPO positive (in ~40%) and often presents with mononeuritis multiplex and cardiac involvement. GPA is cANCA/anti-PR3 positive with necrotising granulomatous inflammation but no asthma/eosinophilia. Renal pauci-immune glomerulonephritis, ANCA positivity, and response to steroids plus cyclophosphamide (or rituximab, per RITUXVAS/RAVE trials) are shared by both ANCA-associated vasculitides and therefore cannot distinguish them. Upper respiratory involvement occurs in both (EGPA causes allergic rhinitis/nasal polyps) so is not discriminating. Per BSR/EULAR, remission induction uses rituximab or cyclophosphamide with glucocorticoids. 🩺

q: A 23-year-old man presents with a 9-month history of low back pain and stiffness that is worst in the early morning, lasts over an hour, and improves with exercise but not rest. He wakes in the second half of the night with pain. Examination shows reduced lumbar flexion (modified Schober's test) and reduced chest expansion. He has had one episode of a painful red eye. CRP is mildly elevated; rheumatoid factor is negative. An MRI of the sacroiliac joints shows bone marrow oedema consistent with active sacroiliitis. Which single mechanism best explains this patient's disease susceptibility?
options: Anti-CCP-mediated citrullinated peptide autoimmunity
Immune-complex deposition activating classical complement
HLA-B27-associated CD8 T-cell and IL-23/IL-17 axis activation
Monosodium urate crystal-induced NLRP3 inflammasome activation
Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody-mediated vasculitis
explain: 🎯 This is ankylosing spondylitis (axial spondyloarthritis): inflammatory back pain (insidious onset <45 years, morning stiffness >30 min, night pain, improvement with exercise not rest), reduced spinal mobility and chest expansion, anterior uveitis (painful red eye), and MRI-confirmed active sacroiliitis. The disease is strongly linked to HLA-B27 (present in ~90% of patients) and driven by the IL-23/IL-17 axis. Mechanism: HLA-B27 (an MHC class I molecule) may misfold in the endoplasmic reticulum (unfolded protein response) and present arthritogenic peptides to CD8 T cells; this, combined with IL-23-driven expansion of IL-17-producing cells at entheses (sites of mechanical stress), causes enthesitis, osteitis and eventually new bone formation (syndesmophytes, bamboo spine). This biology underpins the efficacy of TNF-α and IL-17 inhibitors (secukinumab) per NICE/BSR. Anti-CCP autoimmunity is rheumatoid arthritis; immune-complex/complement is SLE; MSU crystal/NLRP3 inflammasome is gout; ANCA drives small-vessel vasculitis — none explains this seronegative, HLA-B27-linked axial disease. 🩺

q: A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, hypertension treated with a thiazide diuretic, and chronic kidney disease (eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m²) presents with a second attack of acute gout affecting the first metatarsophalangeal joint. His serum urate is 540 μmol/L. The acute attack has now fully settled and he is asymptomatic. He has no known allergies and normal liver function. According to current BSR/NICE guidance, which single option is the most appropriate long-term management to prevent recurrent attacks?
options: Start allopurinol at low dose with colchicine cover and titrate to a urate target below 360 μmol/L
Start high-dose allopurinol 300 mg immediately without prophylactic cover
Avoid all urate-lowering therapy because he has chronic kidney disease
Start febuxostat first-line in preference to allopurinol
Continue the thiazide diuretic and treat only acute attacks with NSAIDs
explain: 🎯 With recurrent gout (≥2 attacks), tophi, or gout with CKD/diuretic use, urate-lowering therapy (ULT) is indicated. Per BSR (2017) and NICE NG219 (2022), allopurinol is first-line, started at a low dose (e.g. 50–100 mg, lower in renal impairment) and titrated up monthly to achieve a target serum urate <360 μmol/L (or <300 μmol/L with tophi/severe disease). Prophylaxis against paradoxical flares with low-dose colchicine (or NSAID) is given during initiation and titration. Mechanism: allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, reducing urate synthesis. Initiating ULT mobilises urate from tissue stores, transiently precipitating flares — hence the need for colchicine cover for up to 6 months. Starting ULT is deferred until the acute attack settles (as here) or, if started during an attack, the attack is still treated. Starting 300 mg without titration risks hypersensitivity and flares. CKD is not a contraindication — dose is simply adjusted. Febuxostat is second-line (reserved for allopurinol intolerance; carries cardiovascular caution per CARES). The thiazide raises urate and should ideally be switched to an alternative antihypertensive. 🩺

q: A 52-year-old woman presents with a 6-week history of progressive symmetrical proximal muscle weakness, struggling to climb stairs and rise from a chair. She has a violaceous rash over her eyelids and erythematous scaly plaques over the knuckles. Creatine kinase is markedly elevated at 4200 U/L. She is found to have anti-Mi-2 antibodies. Given her diagnosis, which single further investigation is most important to prioritise?
options: Anti-Jo-1 antibody testing for antisynthetase syndrome
Nerve conduction studies to exclude a neuropathy
Muscle MRI to guide the site of muscle biopsy
Age-appropriate screening for occult malignancy
Echocardiography to assess for pulmonary hypertension
explain: 🎯 The heliotrope (violaceous eyelid) rash and Gottron's papules (scaly plaques over knuckles) with proximal weakness and raised CK indicate dermatomyositis. A critical association is occult malignancy — dermatomyositis is a recognised paraneoplastic phenomenon (notably ovarian, lung, breast, gastric, colorectal and nasopharyngeal cancers), with greatest risk in the first 1–3 years after diagnosis. Therefore age-appropriate malignancy screening (examination, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, mammography, CA-125/pelvic imaging, and other targeted tests) is the priority. Mechanism: dermatomyositis is a humorally-mediated microangiopathy with complement (C5b-9 membrane attack complex) deposition on endomysial capillaries, causing perifascicular atrophy; tumour antigens may trigger cross-reactive immunity, explaining the paraneoplastic link. Antibody note: anti-Mi-2 associates with classic cutaneous dermatomyositis and a relatively lower cancer risk (anti-TIF1-γ and anti-NXP2 carry the highest malignancy risk), but malignancy screening remains essential in any adult with dermatomyositis. Anti-Jo-1/antisynthetase testing (relevant to ILD/mechanic's hands) and echocardiography are useful but secondary. Muscle MRI/biopsy confirm the diagnosis but the paraneoplastic search most affects outcome. 🩺

q: A 4-year-old boy is referred with a history of recurrent severe bacterial infections since 6 months of age, including two episodes of pneumococcal pneumonia, recurrent otitis media, and one episode of Giardia enteritis. His maternal uncle died in childhood from infection. Examination reveals absent tonsils and no palpable lymph nodes. Blood tests show markedly reduced IgG, IgA and IgM, but a normal lymphocyte count. Flow cytometry shows absent circulating CD19+ B cells with normal T-cell numbers. Which single underlying mechanism best explains this immunodeficiency?
options: Defective CD40 ligand preventing immunoglobulin class switching
Bruton tyrosine kinase mutation arresting B-cell maturation
Failure of T-cell development due to thymic aplasia
Defective NADPH oxidase impairing neutrophil oxidative burst
Complement C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency
explain: 🎯 The picture — a boy with onset after ~6 months (waning maternal IgG), recurrent encapsulated bacterial infections (pneumococcus), Giardia, absent tonsils/lymphoid tissue, panhypogammaglobulinaemia, and absent CD19+ B cells with normal T cells, plus an X-linked family history — is classic X-linked agammaglobulinaemia (Bruton's). The cause is a mutation in Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK). Mechanism: BTK is a cytoplasmic signalling kinase essential for pre-B-cell receptor signalling. Loss of function arrests B-cell development at the pre-B-cell stage in the bone marrow, so mature B cells and plasma cells never form — hence absent circulating CD19+ B cells, absent tonsils/nodes, and failure to produce any immunoglobulin class. T-cell immunity is intact, so viral/fungal handling is relatively preserved (though enteroviral meningoencephalitis and Giardia are notable risks). Treatment is lifelong immunoglobulin replacement. CD40-ligand defect causes X-linked hyper-IgM (high/normal IgM, low IgG/IgA, B cells present). Thymic aplasia is DiGeorge (T-cell defect). NADPH oxidase defect is chronic granulomatous disease (catalase-positive organisms, normal Igs). C1-inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema, not infection susceptibility. 🩺
